title: With Iran war cooling, Trump is refocusing on tariffs | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

“Tariff” may be one of President Donald Trump’s favorite words. But since the war with Iran broke out, it has rarely been part of his vocabulary.

With afragile agreementbetween the United States and Iran offering a path toward ending the monthslong war, tariffs are back on Trump’s agenda. It could get ugly quickly.

Ahead of this week’sG7 Summit in France, Trump threatened to enact a 100% tax on French wine if France’s President Emmanuel Macron didn’t ditch a 3% digital service tax. The tax is especially hard-hitting for US tech giants such as Amazon, Alphabet, Apple and Meta.

“I asked him not to charge American companies, and if they do, I have no choice but to charge a 100% tariff on all Champagnes and all wines coming out of France,” Trump told the New York Post in aninterviewpublished Monday.

Trump has been making these kinds of threats since the tax was enacted in 2019. Before his latest warning, he threatened in January tointroduce a 200% tariffon French wines and Champagne after Macron signaled he wouldn’t join Trump’s “Board of Peace” on Gaza.

But, for a variety of reasons Trump hasn’t followed through with those threats.

The White House denied any connection between the agreement with Iran and Trump’s French tariff warning. “There isn’t a pivot here; the President is responding to an issue on which he has clearly staked a position on,” White House spokesperson Kush Desai told CNN in a statement.

Beyond French wines and Champagne, which risk broader retaliation from the European Union, Trump has also vowed to increase levies on EU cars, claiming the trading bloc violated an agreement inked last summer. On top of that, the USTR recently proposed tariffs starting at 12.5% on all goods from Japan, China and Indiaover alleged forced labor concerns.

These tariffs are expected to take effect after a temporary 10% import tax expires next month.

Trump introduced sweeping tariffs last April, paralyzing businesses and freezing their decision-making and hiring. The majority of the levies were subsequentlystruck down by the Supreme Court.

Now, more than a year later, the effects of tariffs on the labor market are just beginning to fade. Employers who hesitated to hire more workers due to the uncertain trade climate have started to hire again: The US economy has added an average of 188,000 jobs a month over the past three months — a far cry fromlast year, when fewer than 10,000 jobs were added each month.

But annual inflation, which measured just 2.4% before the US-Israeli war with Iran,surged to 4.2% last month,the highest rate in three years, according to the Consumer Price Index. On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.5%, with the higher cost of energy accounting for 60% of the increase.

So the prospect of a slew of new import duties comes at an especially precarious time.

But economists have been taking comfort in an underlying inflation measure that strips out food and energy prices. That gauge, known as “core” inflation, clocked in at 0.2% on a monthly basis and 2.9% in May.

It signifies that – for now at least – higher energy prices generally haven’t pushed prices of other goods and services significantly higher since the start of the war. That’s not always the case, given energy is one of the major expenses for businesses, and when prices go up, they often pass it along to consumers.

The jury is still out on that, even if the Strait of Hormuz returns to pre-war oil tanker traffic.

“We believe the US is facing a persistent inflation problem, in part because of the Middle East conflict but also the entrenchment of pandemic-era inflation into services prices,” economists at BNP Paribas wrote in a note last week.
